newsitem.title: CROATIA: INTERVIEW - Croatia to seek more foreign funds.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Croatia to seek more foreign funds.

text.p: Croatia, having applied for sovereign credit rating last month, is to launch an agressive campaign to lure in more foreign investors, the head of the government's investment agency said on Monday.

Vanja Kalogjera of the Croatian Investment Promtion Agency (CIPA), set up this summer, said the government was aiming for investors primarily in the energy and infrastructure sectors to improve the basis for the ex-Yugoslav republic's industrial recovery.
"Our primary target is to attract large institutional investors to help finance projects in the fields of energetics and infrastructure," Kalogjera told Reuters in an interview.

He said projects such as the construction of power plants or new highways could not be financed by cash-strapped Croatia alone, still suffering the financial aftermath of four years of war in the region that stopped last year.

The agency would also actively seek foreign partners interested in setting up companies in the country's five free trade zones -- the ports of Rijeka, Ploce and Sibenik, and in Osijek and Krapina in the north.
"Parliament passed a law on free trade zones this summer and we already had contacts with two Asian concerns -- Daewoo and Hyundai -- which are interested in concessions," Kalogjera said.
He said the agency's rough estimate was that some $1.8 billion of foreign capital entered the country since it broke from foreign communist Yugoslavia in 1991, compared to next to nothing before.
That would put Croatia in fourth position of foreign investment per capita among the reform countries of eastern Europe, after Hungary, Czech Republic and Slovenia, he said.
Big investors in Croatia include Ericsson, Societe Suisse de Cement, Siemens, Interbrew and ABB and most projects were centered in the areas of electronics, machine industry, cement and beverages.

After the first mildly successful tourist season in five years last summer, foreign investors also were beginning to discover hotel companies on Croatia's scenic Adriatic coast, Kalogjera said. Most analysts predict a speedy recovery of the once lucrative tourist industry in just a few years.
"There is interest in shipyards and investing in wood-processing," Kalogjera added. "And we have a flood of offers for opening big shopping malls, mainly around Zagreb."

He said Croatia expected to enter a period of steady growth amid the overall monetary stability achieved in the past three years. "Our main advantage over other Eatern European countries is skilled labour," Kalogjera said.
He added Croatia also was a comparatively open country, with a legal framework designed to protect and attract foreign investments in the long run.
"There are no restrictions on foreign investment, except in the defence industry, and transfers of profits are constitutionally guaranteed," he said.
